title: The Cost of a Hostile Boss
text:
In 2000 the management researcher Bennett Tepper published a study of what he called abusive supervision: bosses who repeatedly ridicule, belittle, blame and give the silent treatment to their subordinates, without necessarily using physical aggression. He surveyed several hundred working adults in an American city and then surveyed them again about six months later.

At the first survey, participants described how often their supervisor engaged in such behavior. Six months later, Tepper checked who had left their jobs and asked those who remained about their attitudes and well-being.

Employees with more abusive supervisors were more likely to have quit. Those who stayed reported lower satisfaction with their jobs and their lives, less commitment to their organization, more depression, anxiety and emotional exhaustion, and more conflict between work and family life. The effects were stronger for people who felt they had few other job options, who were stuck with the abusive boss. Tepper found that a sense of being treated unfairly helped explain the damage.
lesson: A boss's contempt does not stay at the office: it follows people home. Treat everyone with basic respect, especially those who cannot easily leave.
source: Tepper, B. J. (2000). Consequences of abusive supervision. Academy of Management Journal, 43(2), 178-190.
